chapter: Eddie Heywood, the organ and later work
title: Eddie Heywood and "Begin the Beguine"
summary: Heywood returned from Europe, played Village Vanguard and developed his bass figuration on "Begin the Beguine," working off-nights alongside Ramirez.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: We've got a good (?) to go. You don't really want to say anything more about Bebop. But the pianists like... For instance, at the beginning of the Forties Eddie Heywood came on the scene. He had a big influence.
Well, Eddie Heywood came within the time that I went to Europe. Eddie had come back from Europe... He had gone to Europe with...
But it was after you came back that he sort of had his big hits, with "Begin The Beguine" and things like that.
Well, that happened after he left Benny Carter. I remember hearing the (?) Rock, a broadcast...
I heard that in Hollywood over the American Network or something.
What did you think of Eddie as a piano player?

He was inventive. He played plain diatonic piano. He had ideas and he learned things, and he pushed them. So he started at the Village Vanguard. And then he had his arrangement of "Begin The Beguine" with a drummer named Kay(?) Quennel(?). Because I used to play on the off-nights down there at the time. They hired me and Josh White, Ann(?) Robinson, Burl Ives... Who was the other English troubadour?

Oh, gee, he was one of the first ones... He later influenced Eddie Heywood's arrangement for "Begin The Beguine." This was the bass figuration. It took off, you know, and it became one of his main numbers that he used to do as a solo.

I can remember Eddie was the first one to record "Lover Man."
